PITTSBURGH — The Pittsburgh Pirates won't finish the 2026 season with playoff baseball and it's a let down for every player, especially Paul Skenes.
The Pirates' starting pitcher, who ended his third MLB season, hasn't been a part of a postseason team yet, with the 2026 team eliminated a week ago.
Skenes and the Pirates did avoid a losing season, but the ace is done with coming up short and wants to be a part of a playoff squad, something he envisions in Pittsburgh.
"That's cool. We all wanted to play in October," Skenes said. "Like I said, I think our best baseball is ahead of us, I thought there was a lot of kind of unfortunate stuff that happened this year. Stuff that was just out of our control. Guys getting hurt and stuff like that. I think it'd be a different picture if stuff like that didn't happen. So it's tough.
"This is my third year, and every year, at the end, we’re talking about ‘What’s it going to look like for next year,’ and I’m tired of it. We are in a good position for next year, I know that, but it’s gonna be tough to think about that again for a whole offseason.”
Skenes Hoping For Better in 2027
The Pirates were competitive throughout the 2026 season and can clinch a winning season with a win in their final two games against the Detroit Tigers at Comerica Park, on either Sept. 26 or Sept. 27.
Pittsburgh last had a winning season in 2018, 82-79, and hasn't made the postseason since 2015, the second-longest streak in baseball to the Los Angeles Angels (2014).
The Pirates have had little success in recent history, with this just the fifth non-losing season in the past 34 years, with three postseason appearances from 2013-15 and a record 20 straight losing seasons from 1993-2012.
2026 was a much better season for the Pirates, who put together a roster that had postseason potential.
The Pirates had one of the best lineups in baseball before the All-Star break, with offseason additions in second baseman Brandon Lowe and slugger Ryan O'Hearn excelling, internal improvements from center fielder Oneil Cruz, left fielder Bryan Reynolds, first baseman Spencer Horwitz, catcher Endy Rodríguez and third baseman Nick Gonzales, plus breakout rookies in shortstop Konnor Griffin and right fielder Esmerlyn Valdez.
Pittsburgh fell short of their goal due to injuries to their best hitters, a bullpen that struggled and a starting rotation that was inconsistent.
The Pirates have a much better bullpen following the trade deadline and a starting rotation that should be in a better position next season, so there is reason for optimism that they can finally break through.
"I don't know, and that's going to be another off-season thing," Skenes said about what the Pirates need to do next season. "You know, I don't. I don't think there's anything that needs to be completely overhauled."
Skenes Faces Important Offseason
Skenes has a big offseason, himself, after falling short of his National League Cy Young Award season in 2025.
He posted a 10-11 record in 32 starts, a 3.82 ERA over 174.1. innings pitched, 200 strikeouts to 49 walks, a .227 BAA and a 1.12 WHIP.
Skenes' ERA was almost twice what it was last season, although his expected ERA (3.28) was 10th-best in baseball.
There were some mechanical issues and a drop in velocity for Skenes this season, as well as an early start due to the World Baseball Classic, but with a full offseason ahead of him, he's confident he can fix those issues and help lead the Pirates back to the postseason in 2027.
“I think my best baseball is ahead of me, and I think our best baseball is ahead of us," Skenes said. "Got a long offseason and have the chance to sit down and look at all the stuff. It’s really easy to get emotional and kind of let emotions bleed into some stuff during the season. To be able to sit back and kinda look at the big picture rather than the day-to-day, short-term view of it that takes over in-season, that will be good.”

Las Grandes Ligas de Béisbol (MLB, por sus siglas en inglés) revelaron las 20 camisetas de peloteros más vendidas de la temporada 2026.
En la lista figura un solo pelotero venezolano: Ronald Acuña Jr., de los Bravos de Atlanta, quien ocupa la cuarta posición. En 2025, Acuña Jr. también figuró en este listado, pero en el puesto 11.
La publicación, difundida por la MLB en su cuenta de Instagram, reveló que el japonés Shohei Ohtani, de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles, encabeza la lista de las camisetas más vendidas.
En cuanto a los equipos, los Dodgers de Los Ángeles son los que cuentan con más jugadores en la lista, con cuatro: Ohtani, Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts y Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
¿Quiénes son los 20 peloteros con las camisetas más vendidas en 2026?
De acuerdo con la lista difundida por la MLB, estas son las 20 camisetas más vendidas de la temporada 2026:
- Shohei Ohtani, Dodgers de Los Ángeles.
- Aaron Judge, Yankees de Nueva York.
- Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cachorros de Chicago.
- Ronald Acuña Jr., Bravos de Atlanta.
- Fernando Tatis Jr., Padres de San Diego.
- Freddie Freeman, Dodgers de Los Ángeles.
- Bryce Harper, Filis de Filadelfia.
- Mookie Betts, Dodgers de Los Ángeles.
- Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Dodgers de Los Ángeles.
- Juan Soto, Mets de Nueva York.
- Corey Seager, Texas Rangers.
- Vladimir Guerrero Jr., Toronto Blue Jays.
- Adley Rutschman, Medias Rojas de Boston.
- Kyle Schwarber, Filis de Filadelfia.
- Paul Skenes, Piratas de Pittsburgh.
- Cal Raleigh, Marineros de Seattle.
- Elly De La Cruz, Rojos de Cincinnati.
- Jackson Merrill, Padres de San Diego.
- Nolan Arenado, Arizona Diamondbacks.
- Munetaka Murakami, Chicago White Sox.
Shohei Ohtani encabeza por cuarto año consecutivo
El japonés Shohei Ohtani, de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles, volvió a ser el jugador con la camiseta más vendida de las Grandes Ligas, una posición que ocupa por cuarto año consecutivo.
Ohtani se convirtió así en el primer jugador en encadenar cuatro temporadas como líder en ventas de camisetas desde que MLB comenzó a registrar este dato en 2010, reseñó la agencia de noticias EFE este viernes 25 de septiembre.
Desde 2023, los aficionados han comprado la camiseta Nike de Ohtani más que cualquier otra en Estados Unidos, Japón y el resto del mundo, consolidando al jugador japonés como la figura con mayor demanda comercial entre los peloteros de las Grandes Ligas.
El listado, elaborado a partir de las ventas de camisetas Nike realizadas a través de Fanatics, incluido MLBShop.com, desde el Día Inaugural de la temporada 2026, sitúa al capitán de los Yankees de Nueva York, Aaron Judge, en el segundo puesto y al jardinero de los Cachorros de Chicago Pete Crow-Armstrong en el tercero.

DETROIT — Doc Emrick is most famous for his work as a Hall of Fame hockey broadcaster, but he’s always been a baseball fan at heart, especially when it comes to his beloved Pirates.
In fact, Emrick can pinpoint the exact day his Pirates fandom was solidified, which would surprise absolutely no one who’s ever listened to him call a hockey game.
The day was Aug. 9, 1959. The Pirates beat the Cubs at Wrigley Field in 10 innings, and Elroy Face earned the win. Emrick, who grew up in Fontaine, Ind. was there to witness it.
Initially intrigued by hearing Bob Prince call Pirates games on the radio, Emrick passed the point of no return when he saw the team win in person.
“I was hooked,” Emrick said Friday before the Pirates played the Tigers at Comerica Park. Emrick lives in St. Clair, Mich., about an hour north.
“I got to see three World Series championships, and the last guy who was on the mound when they won a World Series was Kent Tekulve. I’m proud to know him and have been around him down at fantasy camp.”
Emrick said it’s been about five years since he attended a Major League game but was thrilled to be around it live again. He watches every Pirates game back home and will join the SportsNet Pittsburgh broadcast alongside Greg Brown and John Wehner.
Predictably, Emrick was all smiles pregame while meeting with manager Don Kelly and saying hello to a few players, including noted hockey fan Spencer Horwitz.
“This is a special treat for me,” Emrick said. “The fact that I can see the Rock and Brownie and actually sit in with them [Friday], that’s special to me.”
Emrick participated in Pirates fantasy camp back in 2012 and encouraged anyone on the fence about doing it to take the plunge.
Starting with their Opening Day homers, Brandon Lowe and Ryan O’Hearn have been two of Emrick’s favorite players to watch this season, for how they seem to come through at important times.
On the pitching side, Emrick obviously enjoys watching Paul Skenes. But Mason Montgomery’s ascent this season has also been a pleasant surprise, leading Emrick to drop an obscure Ryne Duren (Google it) reference that’s very uniquely him.
“I like to see pitches thrown 100 or 101 miles per hour, because I could only imagine that when I was watching back in an earlier era,” Emrick said. “There was a pitcher for the New York Yankees that had Coke bottle glasses named Ryne Durne, and Yogi Berra felt that he probably pitched 90 miles an hour.
“Nobody wanted to bat against him, especially on a cold day. That was 90 [mph] and considered to be off the charts back then. The standard now is so much different.
“But to have confidence in a closer that comes out of the bullpen and you realize he’s probably got this thing, that’s really, really good. … I wish he could pitch every game. But you can’t expect that with that kind of velocity, for somebody to pitch every game.”
As for Skenes, Emrick enjoys how much attention he generates around MLB, basically as a point of pride for Pittsburgh. Emrick also isn’t upset that Skenes’ 2026 performance failed to meet previous standards set. In Emrick’s mind, that would’ve been darn near impossible.
“The first couple of years, the standard was so high,” Emrick said. “How is a human being going to rise above that for a third year in a row? Some of these recent outings that he’s had have been spectacular. It’s something to look forward to for the future.”
Emrick retired in October 2020 after 47 years of broadcasting hockey, which included the Stanley Cup Final 22 times. Given the Penguins’ success, Emrick was a regular presence in Pittsburgh and typically tried to work Pirates references into his hockey broadcasts.
There are also Pittsburgh ties with Emrick having taught speech and broadcasting at Geneva College, which basically makes him an honorary Yinzer.
Emrick said he appreciates Pittsburgh being so welcoming, along with the athletic success the city has enjoyed over the years.
“I’m just glad to be around you folks and travel into Pittsburgh now and then,” Emrick said. “I was thinking the other day, the city of Pittsburgh has had so many wonderful athletes in football, baseball and hockey. It’s easy to get spoiled. Not every city has that many that have been that prominent. And they tend to stay around there, don’t they?
“There’s not an edge to people in Pittsburgh. There’s just a general feeling that’s good.”

PITTSBURGH (WAFB) - Former LSU star Paul Skenes ended his season by making Pittsburgh Pirates history.
Then Livvy Dunne made sure one online critic knew about it.
Skenes recorded his 200th strikeout of the season Thursday in his final start of 2026, becoming the first Pirates starter with consecutive 200-strikeout seasons since Bob Veale accomplished the feat from 1964 through 1966.
The right-hander entered the seventh inning against the St. Louis Cardinals sitting at 199 strikeouts.
Skenes struck out Leo Bernal for No. 200 before being removed from the game.
He finished the afternoon allowing one run on three hits and two walks while striking out eight over 6 1/3 innings. Pittsburgh went on to win 2-1.
Skenes finished the season with a 3.82 ERA and exactly 200 strikeouts across 32 starts.
“It was a grind. It was definitely a grind,” Skenes said after the game.
The former LSU national champion acknowledged that his 2026 season did not match the standard of his previous two years but said he believes his best baseball is still ahead.
Livvy Dunne responds to Skenes critic
Former LSU gymnast and social media personality Livvy Dunne later shared photos highlighting moments from Skenes’ season.
One commenter responded, “Tell Paul to lock in.”
Dunne kept her answer short.
“200ks btw,” she replied.
The response came hours after Skenes reached the milestone in Pittsburgh’s final home game of the season.
Skenes and Dunne both became stars while competing at LSU.
Skenes helped lead LSU baseball to the 2023 national championship before the Pirates selected him with the No. 1 overall pick in the MLB Draft. Dunne competed for LSU gymnastics and was part of the program’s 2024 national championship team.
Skenes won the National League Rookie of the Year award after his first major league season and followed it by winning the NL Cy Young Award in 2025.
Despite a more difficult 2026 season, Skenes ended it with a milestone few pitchers in Pirates history have matched.
“I think my best baseball is ahead of me and I think our best baseball is ahead of us,” Skenes said.

Pirates beat the Cardinals 2-1 to secure their first non-losing season since 2018
Ronny Simon raced home on Spencer Horwitz's eighth inning sacrifice fly and the Pittsburgh Pirates assured themselves of the club's first non-losing season in eight years with a 2-1 win over the St. Louis Cardinals on Thursday.
Simon reached on a walk by Ryne Stanek (2-3), advanced to second on a wild pitch and scooted to third when the throw from catcher Ivan Herrera skipped into center field for an error. Horwitz's flyball to center was plenty deep enough for Simon to score.
Luke Weaver (4-1) got the final out of the eighth for Pittsburgh. Mason Montgomery struck out the side in the ninth for his 17th save in 19 chances as Pittsburgh improved to 81-78 with three games to go. The club's previous non-losing season came in 2018 when it won 82 games.
Reigning NL Cy Young Award winner Paul Skenes ended an uneven year by his standards with 6 1/3 excellent innings in his 32nd and final start.
The 24-year-old, whose performance this year has been met with mild criticism locally, allowed one run, three hits and two walks and six strikeouts. He received a loud ovation when he was removed by manager Don Kelly after recording his 200th strikeout of the season when Cardinals designated hitter Leo Bernal was caught looking leading off the seventh.
Skenes became just the second pitcher in the franchise's 145-year history to reach 200 strikeouts in consecutive seasons. He finished 10-11 with a 3.82 ERA, nearly double the MLB-leading 1.97 ERA he posted in 2025.
St. Louis fell to 77-82, assured of consecutive losing seasons for the first time since the shortened 1994 and 1995 seasons.
Alec Burleson hit his 24th homer of the season in the first inning for the Cardinals.
Up next
The Cardinals wrap up the season with a three-game set at NL Central champion Milwaukee while Pittsburgh heads to Detroit to face the Tigers.

Paul Skenes will make his final start of a disappointing season as he tries to lead the Pittsburgh Pirates to a win this afternoon against the St. Louis Cardinals in the decisive contest of a three-game series.
Skenes (10-11, 3.91 ERA) will attempt to help the Pirates (80-78) secure their first non-losing season since 2018. It would be only their second non-losing mark since 2015, which was the last time they made the playoffs. Pittsburgh is playing its home finale.
The 2025 National League Cy Young Award winner will oppose Cardinals right-hander Kyle Leahy (10-5, 3.65) as St. Louis (77-81) tries to win for the third time in four games. The Cardinals need to prevail in all four of their remaining games to avoid a second straight losing season.
Skenes has seen his ERA nearly double from the 1.97 he posted last season, while his fastball velocity has dipped from 98.1 mph to 96.8 mph.
This week, Skenes stated he thinks pitching for Team USA in March during the World Baseball Classic may have contributed to his drop in fastball speed and his struggles this season.
“Usually, that time of year, you’re kind of ramping up and it’s a little bit slow. You can kind of get onto the slope and find your body,” Skenes said. “One live (batting practice), you’re topping at 97 (mph), and then the next you’re 98, 99. And that wasn’t the case this year. … Looking back, I don’t think that really helped.”
Skenes had a stretch of nine starts from May 17-July 1 during which he went 0-6 with a 5.36 ERA and the Pirates lost every time he pitched. During his past 13 starts since then, Skenes is 4-3 with a 4.31 ERA across 71 innings, with Pittsburgh going 8-5 in that span.
The 24-year-old LSU product gave up five runs on six hits, including two home runs, over six innings last Friday against the Kansas City Royals in his most recent start. He struck out seven and walked one in a no-decision.
Skenes is 0-5 with a 2.74 ERA in seven career starts against St. Louis. In his lone outing against the Cardinals this season, in Pittsburgh on April 30, he allowed five runs (three earned) on seven hits, including two home runs, while striking out nine and walking none in five innings.
The Cardinals, who clinched the season series against the Pirates with their 5-1 win Wednesday, will look to finish with eight wins in 13 meetings against their National League Central rivals.
Leahy, who has been on an innings limit of late, is coming off one of his poorer outings of the season. He gave up seven runs (six earned) on five hits and three walks and struck out only one in three innings during a 9-1 loss last Friday to the Washington Nationals.
“It’s disappointing. I didn’t make a lot of great pitches,” Leahy said. “I’m going to go through my bullpen with intent to get better as I always do.”
Leahy has not pitched more than three innings in any of his past five starts, with the Cardinals going 1-4 in that stretch. He doesn’t have a win since Aug. 18.
Leahy is 2-0 with a 2.12 ERA in nine career appearances against the Pirates. Both of his starts against Pittsburgh occurred this year. He fired 5⅔ innings of three-run ball at Pittsburgh on April 28 to earn a win, then threw three innings of one-run ball in St. Louis during a no-decision Aug. 29.

Fast forward a season later, on the same date, Skenes fought to keep his ERA under 4.00 in his final start. Skenes finished a bumpy 2026 on a positive note, allowing one run in 6 1/3 innings in the Pirates' 2-1 win over the Cardinals in Thursday afternoon's home finale at PNC Park.
Skenes logged a 3.82 ERA and 200 strikeouts in ‘26, becoming the first Pirates starter with consecutive seasons of 200-plus K’s since Bob Veale (1964-66).
“It was a grind. It was definitely a grind,” Skenes said. “I think it was a good year. I don’t think it was to the caliber of the last two years, but I’m not gonna sit around all offseason thinking about how bad this season was, because I just don’t think that’s true.
“I understand the standard that was set the last couple of years, but I think there was a lot of good, and stuff to get better at. Probably some low-hanging fruit and some other stuff to address in the offseason, but the thing that I’m happiest about is the 32 starts.”
St. Louis took the lead on Skenes in the top of the first with a solo homer by Alec Burleson. After Burleson’s shot, the Pirates (81-78) tied the game in the bottom half of the inning on a single by Brandon Lowe. A stalemate then took place throughout the afternoon.
Skenes mowed down Cardinals batters, recording eight strikeouts and allowing three hits and two walks. He induced soft contact, and even played some defense to turn a 1-6-3 double play to end the fifth inning.
As he trotted out for the sixth with 81 pitches, Skenes retired the side in order. He then came out for the seventh at 90 pitches, and one strikeout away from 200. Skenes told manager Don Kelly that he felt the best he has in a long time, but Kelly didn’t want him over 100 pitches. Skenes took down Leo Bernal for his 200th K before being lifted in favor of reliever Yohan Ramirez with the game knotted at 1.
Skenes has been fairly open about the struggles in 2026 compared to his first two seasons, as his ERA nearly doubled with a dip in velocity. He was proud of grinding out 32 starts, and he learned plenty about his controllables going forward.
“We've talked a lot about nobody expects more from Paul Skenes than Paul Skenes expects from himself,” Kelly said. “I know what everybody sees every day is the same guy. Comes in, focused, works his butt off. And it was tough for him going through that. I think any time any of us go through anything that's tough in life, we learn from it, grow from it, and there's no doubt that Paul is going to as well. He has this year. I think today was evidence of that, just finishing on such a strong note, throwing the ball extremely well. Excited for him this offseason and excited for what he's gonna be next year.”
Skenes analyzed the idea of an 11-month season, saying he’ll begin throwing again likely near the end of October. A mental breather is needed, sometimes even more than a physical one.
The road was bumpy. Skenes has heard the clichés of being better off after facing adversity. He definitely doesn’t think it will hurt. But he won’t know if 2026 is an anomaly until he’s back on the mound in an MLB game once again.
“I think my best baseball is ahead of me and I think our best baseball is ahead of us,” Skenes said. “Got a long offseason and have the chance to sit down and look at all the stuff. It’s really easy to get emotional and kind of let emotions bleed into some stuff during the season. To be able to sit back and kinda look at the big picture rather than the day-to-day, short-term view of it that takes over in-season, that will be good.”

PITTSBURGH – Paul Skenes' perplexing 2026 season came to an end on Thursday afternoon at PNC Park.
Skenes started against the Cardinals in his team's final home game of the 2026 season. The right-hander held St. Louis to one run on three hits with two walks and eight strikeouts in a 2-1 Pirates' win, their 81st of the season.
"He threw the ball great," said manager Don Kelly.
Skenes was at 90 pitches with seven strikeouts through six innings, but he trotted out back to the mound for one more batter in the seventh inning. Skenes struck out Cardinals designated hitter Leo Bernal, which gave him 200 punchouts on the season. He became the third pitcher in Pirates history to have two consecutive seasons with at least 200 strikeouts.
"I was pushing to go back out," Skenes said of chasing his 200th strikeout. "I think if I had gotten a strikeout in the sixth there, I wouldn't have gone back out. But I basically asked for one hitter and [Kelly] gave it to me. I appreciate that."
Skenes entered the season with high expectations after emerging as perhaps the game's top starting pitcher. But the reigning National League Cy Young winner fell short of the heavy standard he set through his first two years with the Pirates. Skenes finished his third big-league big season 10-11 with a 3.82 ERA in 32 starts.
Despite an ERA jump of nearly two full points, Skenes feels like he still had a good – albeit challenging – season.
"It was a grind. It was definitely a grind," Skenes said of his season. "I think it was a good year. I don't think it was to the caliber of the last two years, but I'm not gonna sit around all offseason thinking about how bad this season was, because I just don't think that's true. I understand the standard that was set the last couple of years, but I think there was a lot of good and stuff to get better at. … but the thing that I'm happiest about is the 32 starts."
A disastrous first start of the year on Opening Day in New York was quickly erased by a dominant stretch through the middle of May. Back-to-back eight-inning outings capped off a stretch of nine starts in which Skenes combined for a 1.09 ERA. But beginning with his start against the Phillies on May 17, Skenes combined for a 4.56 ERA over his final 23 outings. The Pirates went 9-14 in those games.
From his time in college at LSU to a brief stint in the minor leagues before his two-year dominance in the big leagues, Skenes had never gone through the adversity that he endured this season. While the results weren't always the same as what they've been, Skenes' consistency remained in his off-the-field work through the challenges.
"We've talked a lot about nobody expects more from Paul Skenes than Paul Skenes expects from himself," Kelly said of his ace. "I know what everybody sees everyday is the same guy. Comes in, [is] focused, works his butt off. And it was tough for him going through that."
Now that his season is over Skenes, will take time to shift his focus towards 2027. Despite taking a step back this season, he still feels like better days are ahead. And given the improvement the Pirates have shown this year, he feels the same way about what lies ahead for his team.
"I think my best baseball is ahead of me and I think our best baseball is ahead of us. Got a long offseason and have the chance to sit down and look at all the stuff. It's really easy to get emotional and kind of let emotions bleed into some stuff during the season. To be able to sit back and kinda look at the big picture rather than the day-to-day, short-term view of it that takes over in-season, that will be good."

item.content:encoded:
What are we supposed to do with Paul Skenes? Through June of this season, he was just about the best young pitcher we'd seen since Dwight Gooden 40 years ago. But over his past 15 starts, he has a 5.06 ERA, with declining velocity to go along with mediocre (at best) production.
My typical inclination is to give Skenes the benefit of the doubt. Sure, I wouldn't want to rank him as a top-three SP like I was coming into the season, but given the much longer track record of him as one of the best pitchers in baseball, he deserves some benefit of the doubt, right?
I think so. I certainly won't rank him as if he's a 5.00-plus ERA pitcher. But man, it just doesn't feel like this is a normal slump. Skenes admitted to tweaking his mechanics throughout the season to try to rediscover his old form, and nothing seems to have helped much. He had a stretch in August where it looked like he might be figuring things out, but then he allowed five runs in his most recent start last week against the Royals of all teams. He has one start with more than five strikeouts in his past seven starts and just six with more than six strikeouts since his season took that turn in late June. He hasn't looked like an impact pitcher for an awfully long time.
And, honestly, the fact that both Skenes and the Pirates have maintained he is healthy throughout this whole stretch doesn't even make me feel better. If Skenes was battling through some kind of lingering-but-manageable injury, I could at least move forward with the hope that a fully healthy offseason would get him back on track. But this? A complete collapse without a good explanation – I don't buy the World Baseball Classic as a cause for why Skenes suddenly stopped pitching well three months after making two starts there, sorry – is a lot harder to make sense of.
Players typically don't just stop being good at 25 years old without an injury, but that's less true of pitchers, certainly. What makes pitchers so frustrating is that they often do just stop being good seemingly overnight; the other side of that coin, of course, is that sometimes pitchers just start being really good seemingly overnight. I can't dismiss Skenes' sudden dropoff quite as easily as I can someone like Vladimir Guerrero's, even though both are plenty concerning.
I haven't finished my pitcher rankings yet – keep an eye out for my first batch of rankings for 2027 next week! – but there's no way I can rank Skenes as a top-12 option at this point. Top 24 seems possible, but at this point, I'm leaning toward dropping him a bit below that. Taking such action could be a huge mistake, and a huge win for anyone who does take the risk on Skenes bouncing back. But right now, I'm not ready to make that bet.
The toughest players to rank at starting pitcher
Garrett Crochet, Red Sox
Woof, that's a big one up top. Crochet was a consensus top-three starting pitcher entering the season, then struggled for a month, went on the IL with shoulder inflammation, and still hasn't returned after suffering an additional lat injury. At this point, it seems like we'll see him in the postseason, though likely only as a reliever. That, frankly, won't tell us much about what to expect from the quality of his stuff as a starter in 2027, nor about his ability to actually stay on the mound, regardless of how effective he will be.
Crochet is unquestionably one of the most talented pitchers in baseball, a massive lefty with a funky delivery and a deep arsenal full of unhittable stuff. He's shown the ability to adapt his arsenal and improve both across and within seasons. He has even shown the ability to hold up to an ace workload—exactly one time in nearly a decade, dating back to college.
And there's the issue. Even if he's dominant this postseason and healthy next spring, does that tell us anything about his ability to stay healthy? Of course not. Any price for Crochet will be a calculated risk. If you draft him as the seventh pitcher off the board, there's room for significant upside; if you draft him 47th, it could be a totally wasted pick. The specific injury Crochet has been dealing with isn't the kind we typically associate with ruining a pitcher's career – this isn't a blown elbow or some structural shoulder issue that requires surgery – but it might be the precursor to all that. Or it might not be.
The uncertainty here, combined with the upside, makes Crochet maybe the toughest pitcher to evaluate for 2027. With that said, no matter where I end up ranking him, I don't think anything we see from him this postseason could move him up in the rankings, short of him emerging as an ace starter again.
Logan Gilbert, Mariners
Gilbert just hasn't seemed quite right all season, but it's not like anything specifically looks wrong. When you go pitch-by-pitch in his arsenal, everything mostly still looks good, with four different pitches with a 30% whiff rate or better, plus an above-average whiff rate on the four-seamer and pretty good results on balls in play. The four-seamer, splitter, slider, and changeup all rate out well by Stuff+, to the point where he actually has the best overall Stuff+ rating of his career, while still rating out well by command.
But his walk rate is up to a career-high mark, his strikeout rate has regressed from his career-best mark in 2025, and he's having as much trouble with homers as ever. It's hard to put your finger on exactly why things have gone wrong for Gilbert, but they undeniably have, resulting in his worst run-prevention marks since his rookie season. My theory is that Gilbert's reintroduction of his cutter and changeup this season has just messed with his feel enough to throw him off-center a bit. Not enough to immediately jump out as a glaring problem, but enough that he hasn't been quite the same guy as the innings have accumulated.
Gilbert is a tinkerer, and he plays in an organization that encourages tinkering, which is no small part of why he has emerged as such a good pitcher in the first place. But I strongly believe in the idea that pitchers can tinker their way out of greatness just as much as they can tinker their way to it, and that's my theory for what's happened with Gilbert. The good news is that the talent still looks intact, and that should be the most important thing. Gilbert and the Mariners will surely spend the offseason trying to figure out exactly why things went wrong and how to fix it, and I'm not going to give up on a pitcher this talented. He still has top-five upside and I'm interested in buying the dip in 2027 if he falls outside of the top 12.
Jesus Luzardo, Phillies
Luzardo was so close to making it through two straight seasons without injuries. Then he started feeling soreness in his left shoulder following a complete-game shutout against the Braves on Sept. 7 and hasn't pitched since. He has been cleared to throw, however, and hasn't even been ruled out for the NL Wild Card series next week, as an MRI showed no structural damage. So, we're kind of in a holding pattern with Luzardo, and it would be really nice to see him look like himself during a deep playoff run. That won't preclude the possibility of injuries derailing his 2027, of course, but it would at least be a sign that the injury is as minor as the team has said it is.
When he was on the mound, Luzardo was better than ever and almost certainly would have established a new career-high in innings – heck, he might have even gotten to 200 innings for the first time. He pitched right to his peripherals nearly across the board and was one of the best strikeout pitchers in baseball. He was a true ace and might have been ranked as a top-five SP in 2027 without the injury concerns. As it stands, you probably can't justify a top-12 price, but it'll be tough to take him outside of the top 24, too.
Whether you'll actually be able to pull the trigger at that price will depend on your personal risk tolerance.
Zack Wheeler, Phillies
For a few weeks there, it looked like Wheeler's age and last year's surgery caught up to him all at once. His velocity crashed scarily in one start and he struggled to the tune of 23 runs in 24.1 innings of work, with the nadir coming on Aug. 24 when he gave up eight runs to the Mariners.
And then he just … fixed it. Beginning with an Aug. 30 start against the Angels, Wheeler hasn't allowed more than three runs in five straight starts, putting up a 1.71 ERA over his past five starts with 40 strikeouts to nine walks in 31.2 innings of work, which is basically exactly how he was pitching before that month-long hiccup immediately preceding it. That doesn't mean there are no concerns about Wheeler, or that we can totally ignore the downside he showed, especially at his age. But he's up to 156 innings with a 3.06 ERA and a 30% strikeout rate for the season.
That's not quite as good as he was before the injury, when he was a consensus top-five SP, and it's probably unfair to expect him to get back to that level again. His stuff isn't quite that good anymore, and it's hard to totally overcome that with pitchability and veteran guile. But you can largely overcome it, and Wheeler has done exactly that. I can't guarantee he won't just lose it entirely this offseason, but with how good he's been under extremely difficult circumstances this season, I don't think it makes much sense to doubt him at this point, either. He probably has to be ranked as a top-12 SP for 2027, despite the red flags and concerns.
Eury Perez, Marlins
It looked like Perez was finally figuring it out. In a 13-start stretch from May 22 through Aug. 22, Perez put up a 1.67 ERA and 0.90 WHIP, with a 28% strikeout rate and 8.4% walk rate, putting most of his biggest flaws throughout his MLB career behind him. That he did this despite missing nearly a month with a hamstring injury (and returning without a real rehab assignment) made it all the more impressive. Perez has long had ace-level upside, and we figured that once it clicked, it would click for good.
Not so much. He has stumbled badly toward the finish line, putting up a 9.67 ERA over his past six appearances (five starts), with his control completely abandoning him (13% walk rate) and his homer issues coming back in a big way. This doesn't mean Perez can't be an ace – maybe he's just running out of steam amid a 30-plus inning jump from 2025 to a new career high of 150 and counting. But it does mean that he hasn't totally figured it out, and that's frustrating for a player with so much talent. He had a 4.25 ERA last season, which we chalked up to rustiness coming back from Tommy John surgery, but he heads into his final start with a 4.14 ERA and the peripherals to back it up.
Of course, Perez will still be just 23 on Opening Day and still has incredible stuff, and we saw how good he can be when it does click in. You can't draft him as if he's figured it out, but I don't think it makes sense to rank him as if he's just the sum of his final numbers this season. He's too talented for that, and he absolutely could be one of the five best pitchers in baseball if he figures it out for a whole season. I'm leaning toward ranking Perez as a top-24 SP for 2027, even if it makes me a bit uncomfortable.
Jared Jones, Pirates
All aboard the Jared Jones hype train! The Pirates have finally taken the restrictors off him and he has responded with the best run of his career, putting up a 1.08 ERA with 35 strikeouts to just four walks in 25 innings during September after a seven-inning, one-hit gem against the Cardinals Tuesday night. Jones has long carried significant promise, but has rarely put together the kind of stretch that did anything more than tantalize and frustrate. And, honestly, it's possible this stretch will turn out to be nothing more than another tantalizing one before another series of frustrating ones. In fact, I'd probably bet on that being the case.
But know this: Jared Jones is going to be drafted as if this stretch is real. I saw Lance Brozdowski, whose analysis I highly respect, say he thinks Jones "should land as a top-20 arm" for 2027 in his newsletter this week, and he won't be alone. Jones has the raw stuff to be an ace – his fastball plays inconsistently because of its shape, but 98 mph is 98 mph, you know – and his control has actually been pretty good this season. That's especially true lately, but a 7.7% walk rate will play anywhere, especially with a near 30% strikeout rate.
Jones obviously has the talent to live up to a top-20 SP price, but I don't think I'll be the one to actually rank him that way. I can definitely see the case for it, but I need a stronger track record before I make that kind of pick. And Jones doesn't have it. Yet.
Logan Webb, Giants
Webb has always been a pretty weird pitcher. I've compared him to Framber Valdez in the past, in that he's an innings-eating, groundball type of ace, but he also shares a seemingly inherent inconsistency with Valdez, too. The final run prevention numbers have been pretty consistent over the years for Webb (before 2026, at least), but the way he got there would change from one year to the next, best exemplified by how he went from a 20.5% strikeout rate in 2024 to a 26.2% mark in 2025. The strikeout rate regressed in 2026, but his control remained nearly as good. He struggled through his worst full season ever, finishing with a 4.3 ERA in just 160.2 innings.
The most troubling thing is that Webb's groundball rate fell to 50.7%, still a very high mark, but also his worst since an eight-game stint as a rookie in 2019. There wasn't a sudden drop in velocity or change in his arm slot we can point to, and his sinker looked about as effective as ever, with a 2-degree average launch angle and .300 wOBA allowed. The biggest change appears to be in his pitch mix, as Webb's sinker usage ticked down in favor of more four-seamers and cutters. Those aren't even bad pitches for him, necessarily, but increasing their usage seems to fundamentally change something about Webb's profile in a way that doesn't work for him. It doesn't help that his sweeper was significantly less effective, dropping to a 24% whiff rate from 29% in 2025.
None of the changes for Webb look irreversible. He's gone through these stretches every season when he loses the feel for one pitch or another for a while, but he usually gets it back. I feel pretty good about his chances of getting the sweeper back and bouncing back in 2027, but the ceiling isn't so high for Webb that the bounce-back potential is worth overlooking the downside we just saw in action. I wouldn't be surprised if he drops down to around 40 in SP ADP, and I'll probably only rank him a little higher than that myself.

item.content:encoded:
The Pirates saw plenty of these games slip away earlier this season. To close their home slate, they snuck away with one over the Cardinals.
Before leaving for a final series in Detroit, the Pirates guaranteed themselves at least a .500 season by scratching out a run in the eighth inning before Mason Montgomery shut the door in a 2-1 victory before 15,822 Thursday at PNC Park.
The Pirates are now 81-78 on the year, as Montgomery notched his 17th save. They finished this homestand 6-3 and improved to 14-7 during a September that has shown what this team is capable of at full strength.
Paul Skenes did not factor into the decision, but he did give the Pirates a quality start and reached 200 strikeouts for a second consecutive season, something a pitcher hasn’t done since the 1960s.
The win helped the Pirates finish their home slate 44-37, marking the ninth winning record at home since PNC Park opened in 2001. Furthermore, it gave Pittsburgh its third straight series victory over St. Louis.
The Pirates have won three consecutive series against the Cardinals just four times since the NL Central was formed in 1994.
Ronny Simon started the decisive rally by drawing a one-out walk. He moved to second when Cardinals reliever Ryne Stanek bounced a splitter, and catcher Ivan Herrera threw wildly to second base, the ball squirting into the outfield.
Spencer Horwitz drove in the run with a sacrifice fly.
The lone blemish against Skenes came in the first inning, when first baseman Alec Burleson tagged him for a solo home run to right-center. It came on a four-seam fastball up, and it was the fifth consecutive solo shot Skenes has permitted.
St. Louis’ lead was short-lived, however, as Oneil Cruz opened the bottom half of the first with a double, stole third and scored on Brandon Lowe’s line-drive single to live, going the other way with an 0-2 pitch.
Skenes’ start was heavy on strikeouts early on, the right-hander fanning six through the first three innings. With just one strikeout over next three, it looked like Skenes might finish the season stuck at 199.
However, Skenes started the seventh inning and got designated hitter Leo Bernall, freezing him on a full-count sinker to become just the second Pirates pitcher with back-to-back seasons of at least 200 strikeouts. Bob Veale had three straight from 1964-66.
As Skenes exited following his 96th pitch of the afternoon, Pirates fans showered him with an ovation.
It wasn’t the season Skenes had wanted. At the same time, he fought through a lot, including fatigue, and still found a way to produce results: a 3.82 ERA, the 12th-most fWAR (4.1) of any pitcher and a FIP of 3.32 prior to Thursday that ranked 13th.
Skenes enjoyed a pretty even distribution of pitches against the Cardinals and had success with all six. His eight strikeouts required five different offerings, while he amassed 15 whiffs, no more than four with any single pitch.
Consistent with when Skenes has found success over the second half, he pitched ahead a lot, throwing 57 of his 90 pitches for strikes and getting to 0-1 against 17 of 22. Thursday represented the 13th quality start of the season for Skenes … but also just the fourth for him (in 12 tries) since the All-Star break.
In 6 1/3 innings, Skenes allowed an earned run on three hits with two walks and eight strikeouts. It was what we’ve come to expect from Skenes and hopefully some sort of building block going into the offseason.
Cruz, shifted up to the leadoff spot for this one, teamed with Konnor Griffin to provide production out of the top two places in the lineup. Those two accounted for four of the Pirates’ seven hits.
This story will be updated.

item.content:encoded:
We’re down to the final days of the 2026 regular season with still quite a number of teams that have something to play for -- including a few who are fighting for their postseason lives.
Such is the case with the Astros and Rangers, who are tied atop the AL West (with Houston owning the tiebreaker); the team that loses the division will most likely miss the playoffs entirely. Elsewhere in the American League, the Guardians and White Sox are still battling for the division title, though the loser of that should slot into the third wild-card spot.
While all the divisions in the National League have been clinched already, the wild-card race, specifically in terms of seeding, is very much heating up, with the Phillies, Cubs and Padres entering play on Wednesday in a three-way tie.
Which clubs will get to keep playing into October? And which will watch their playoff aspirations come to an end?
Our expert panel has ranked every team based on a combination of what we’ve seen so far and what we already knew going into the 162-game marathon that is a full baseball season. We also asked ESPN MLB experts Bradford Doolittle, Buster Olney and Jorge Castillo to weigh in with an observation for all 30 teams.
1. Milwaukee Brewers
Record: 99-59
Previous ranking: 1
With the season down to a handful of games, the Brewers have all but run out of time for Kyle Harrison to recover his first-half form. Harrison was 8-2 with a 3.01 ERA before the break; he’s 2-3 with a 7.80 ERA since. His strikeout rate has remained steady, even as his velocity and movement measures have become more volatile. Meanwhile, his walk rate has more than doubled, and his homers-allowed rate has nearly tripled. Suffice to say, this is not a great combination of trends. Milwaukee has tried to get Harrison back in stride by using him out of the bullpen, but he’s gotten hammered as a reliever. Brewers fans who dreamed of a big three rotation of Jacob Misiorowski, Harrison and Logan Henderson probably need to recalibrate their expectations at this point. -- Doolittle
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
Record: 97-61
Previous ranking: 2
We’re nearing October baseball, and it’s as if the Dodgers are knocking off items on a to-do list. Shohei Ohtani back in the lineup? Check. Edwin Diaz finding his stuff, finally? Check. Will Smith back in the lineup? Check -- and he has an OPS of close to 1.000 this month. Mookie Betts back to being Mookie Betts? Check. Kyle Tucker digging out of his seasonlong slump? Check. L.A. is putting the pieces back together just in time as it begins its effort to become the first NL team to go back-to-back-to-back. -- Olney
3. Tampa Bay Rays
Record: 96-62
Previous ranking: 3
Tampa Bay began the season with the longest odds to win the AL East. On Tuesday, it clinched its first division title since 2021 with a win over the Yankees. The Rays will enter their first postseason since 2023 as the favorites to win the AL pennant behind a distinct home-field advantage at Tropicana Field, a strong pitching staff and a dynamic lineup centered around MVP candidate Junior Caminero, designated hitter Yandy Diaz and first baseman Jonathan Aranda. With a payroll that ranks 28th in the majors, the Rays seek to become the team with the lowest-ranked payroll to ever win the World Series. -- Castillo
4. Atlanta Braves
Record: 93-65
Previous ranking: 5
Atlanta would’ve preferred to get a first-round bye in the playoffs, of course, but the fact that the Brewers and Dodgers seemed to have locked down the No. 1 and No. 2 seeds allows the Braves to treat this last week of the regular season like the last week of spring training. They can plot out the best way to rest their key relievers, assess the progress of Robert Suarez and arrange at-bats for the position players to be primed for the postseason. Meanwhile, the teams the Braves are likely to face in the first round -- the Phillies, Cubs and Padres -- are all still pushing for berths and home-field advantage in the wild-card round. -- Olney
5. New York Yankees
Record: 91-67
Previous ranking: 4
Despite manager Aaron Boone saying on Tuesday that Aaron Judge isn’t expected to return from his calf strain in time for the wild-card round, Judge told ESPN the following day that he does in fact intend to be ready for Game 1. He suffered the injury last Wednesday and was placed on the injured list two days later. The Yankees were initially cryptic about the setback, declining to disclose the severity and Judge’s outlook.
Boone offered some clarity Tuesday when he called it a “moderate strain” and acknowledged that the club does not plan on having him to open the postseason. Judge received a PPP injection Monday. The Yankees hope that will spur recovery. Otherwise, New York faces an uphill challenge to survive in October without its three-time MVP at his best. -- Castillo
6. Chicago Cubs
Record: 87-71
Previous ranking: 6
No player has made more of a second-half leap than Alex Bregman, whose season has just gathered momentum almost daily since the last week of July. That momentum was stopped in its tracks when Bregman suffered facial fractures last weekend when struck by a foul ball. The good news is that the Cubs decided against placing Bregman on the IL, believing he might be ready for the playoffs after.
But even if that proves to be optimistic, Cubs fans can take solace in the presence of icy-cool rookie Pedro Ramirez. The Cubs didn’t drop off much when Dansby Swanson was injured, as Ramirez provided a league-average bat and glove work at both second and third base that has kept an elite Cubs defense on track. You want Bregman in there, for sure -- but Ramirez provides a heck of a Plan B. -- Doolittle
7. San Diego Padres
Record: 88-70
Previous ranking: 8
San Diego’s magic number for clinching a playoff spot is shrinking, allowing general manager A.J. Preller and skipper Craig Stammen the chance to line up their staff for the wild-card series, with options developing. Stammen indicated to reporters that unless Michael King is needed to clinch a playoff spot on the last day of the regular season, he will be held over to start Game 1 of the wild card, wherever that is -- so he wouldn’t necessarily be used Sunday in order to win home-field advantage in the first round of the playoffs.
Additionally, the Padres are in a better position to rest their bullpen, the perceived strength of the team. Adrian Morejon ranks third among all relievers in innings. Rest might be overrated for Mason Miller: He has made 16 appearances on zero days’ rest, and in those games, he has allowed two hits and one earned run in 16⅔ innings, with two walks and 27 strikeouts. -- Olney
8. Philadelphia Phillies
Record: 87-71
Previous ranking: 7
The culture of Philadelphia’s starting pitchers, from Zack Wheeler to Cristopher Sanchez to Aaron Nola, is to pitch deep into games. Unlike so many starters in this generation, Wheeler takes the mound expecting to work into the late innings -- and the Phillies will need this sort of production from the rotation, given the team’s recent bullpen problems. Orion Kerkering, an important part of the relief corps, struggled so badly that he was sent to the minors last week. Jose Alvarado has pitched better down the stretch, and hard-throwing Alex MacFarlane has quickly ascended into an important role in his rookie season in the bullpen. But the Phillies’ rotation will carry the team’s October dreams. -- Olney
9. Boston Red Sox
Record: 85-73
Previous ranking: 9
The Red Sox rewarded Chad Tracy on Tuesday for leading the team’s historic turnaround by removing his interim tag and giving him a three-year contract to continue as manager. Now he’ll look to accomplish what his predecessor Alex Cora couldn’t last year: beating the Yankees on the road in the AL Wild Card Series.
Boston has cooled off since going 32-5 to put itself in playoff position and faces some injury uncertainty going into October. Ceddanne Rafaela returned Tuesday after missing 16 games with a quad injury, and Willson Contreras was hit by a pitch on his right hand last Thursday and is dealing with soreness. On the mound, the Red Sox could receive two significant reinforcements for the bullpen in Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck. Crochet, last season’s AL Cy Young runner-up, has been out with a shoulder injury since late April, while Houck hasn’t appeared in a game in 2026. -- Castillo
10. Cleveland Guardians
Record: 82-76
Previous ranking: 12
Cleveland is, once again, showing its knack for a strong finishing kick. Over the past decade, only the Dodgers have won more September games. For Guardians fans aching for their team’s first title since the Truman administration, October is a higher priority at this point.
Like the White Sox, the first order of business is to secure the AL Central title and the first-round bye likely to go with it. Given the neck-and-neck nature of Cleveland’s battle with Chicago, there likely isn’t going to be much time for manager Stephen Vogt to ease up on the pedal to finish the season. That would be nice to do when it comes to rookie ace Parker Messick, who will finish the season with at least 50 more innings than he has ever thrown in a season. Messick has shown no signs of fatigue, so it may not matter. -- Doolittle
11. Arizona Diamondbacks
Record: 84-74
Previous ranking: 10
Manager Torey Lovullo’s comments in a radio interview last week in which he acknowledged that the Diamondbacks “probably” -- his word -- need to reach the postseason to earn him a contract extension surprised many in the industry, as Lovullo has a strong and long-standing relationship with his boss, Mike Hazen. The Ketel Marte situation has been challenging for the organization, with the team’s highest-paid position player failing to show up to the park, and owner Ken Kendrick has a reputation for being mercurial and demanding. Lovullo’s contract runs out at season’s end, and he and the Diamondbacks agreed they would discuss his status then. -- Olney
12. Chicago White Sox
Record: 81-77
Previous ranking: 11
The White Sox have wobbled down the stretch, but they have not fallen down. It looks like they will join the playoff party, completing an incredible two-year turnaround that saw them go from setting the modern single-season loss record to playing in October.
Barring a face-plant over the last few days of the season, the question of whether the Sox can overtake Cleveland for the AL Central title is the biggest remaining question. It’s impactful, with a first-round bye likely on the line. A bye is a boon for any team, but among likely postseason entrants, it might loom largest for the White Sox. That’s just because of how manager Will Venable has had to stretch his pitching resources to the maximum just to get to this point. A wild-card skip would give his staff at least a little time to regroup before the ALDS begins. -- Doolittle
13. Pittsburgh Pirates
Record: 80-78
Previous ranking: 14
Why did Paul Skenes lapse into baseball’s pitching middle class rather than continue his march toward Cooperstown? There is no bigger task for the Pirates and Skenes this offseason than figuring this out. With one more start to go, he has already allowed more runs this season than he did in his first two seasons combined. To be sure, it’s not all on Skenes, whose expected ERA, 3.27 per Statcast, is unusually divergent from his actual ERA (3.91). Still, even a 3.27 ERA is a far cry from the level of effectiveness Skenes flashed before this season. Why? Finding the answer to that question could prove to be the biggest addition Pittsburgh makes this winter. -- Doolittle
14. Texas Rangers
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 16
With eyes on the disappointing Mariners and Yordan Alvarez’s Triple Crown watch, the Rangers quietly remained in contention in the historically dreadful AL West all summer. Following three straight losses, they now find themselves tied atop the division with Houston. Texas will host the Mets in a series finale Thursday before finishing the season with three games in Minnesota. The Rangers will need to finish with a better record than the Astros, who own the tiebreaker, to reach the postseason for the first time since winning the 2023 World Series. -- Castillo
15. Houston Astros
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 13
The Astros fired general manager Dana Brown last month and are under .500 with four games remaining ... but they still have a real chance to win the division. That’s the AL West in 2026. The Astros finish the regular season with a four-game series in West Sacramento against an A’s team that has an MLB-worst run differential. The bad news: The Astros head there tied atop the division. The good news: They hold the tiebreaker over Texas. In the background over the last few days of the season: Alvarez’s push to become the first player to win a Triple Crown since Miguel Cabrera in 2013. -- Castillo
16. Toronto Blue Jays
Record: 77-82
Previous ranking: 15
The Blue Jays did not replicate their 2025 magic in 2026, largely due to injuries and their offense falling off a cliff. They finished last season fourth in the majors with a 112 wRC+; this season, they’re tied for 24th with a 95 wRC+. The dropoff starts with Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and George Springer. Guerrero has nine home runs -- and, inexplicably, just one at home -- with a .695 OPS in the first year of a 14-year, $500 million contract extension. Springer, who reversed a precipitous decline to hit 32 home runs with a .959 OPS last season, has 15 home runs with a .730 OPS in 124 games this year -- and he’s a free agent after this season. Whether Springer re-signs or not, a rebound in 2027 starts with Guerrero sparking an offense that is tied for last in home runs in 2026. -- Castillo
17. Miami Marlins
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 18
Here’s the good news about the Marlins’ 2026 season: They hung around all year, battling among the contenders and having some individual successes. Here’s what’s not-so-great about where they stand right now: It’s hard to identify the players who could lead a Miami breakout into full-scale contention with the best NL teams.
Otto Lopez had an excellent season, but he’ll turn 28 years old next week and his OPS is under .800. Griffin Conine is the one player on the team with an OPS over .800, and he’s 29. Sandy Alcantara reestablished himself as a rotation leader, but he’s 31. Eury Perez has flashes of dominance and is just 23, but he’s got an injury history and will finish this season with an ERA over 4.00. More depth and more talent is needed for the Marlins to take the next step. -- Olney
18. Baltimore Orioles
Record: 78-81
Previous ranking: 19
Another disappointing season in Baltimore has already prompted some changes in the front office, but not at the top. President of baseball operations Mike Elias is expected to return in 2027. One move his front office got right was signing Pete Alonso last winter. The first baseman, who has played in every game this season, hit his 40th home run of the season in Monday’s win over the Blue Jays. He clearly isn’t why the Orioles aren’t going to the postseason for the second straight year.
Baltimore’s young position player core has not lived up to the hype, while the pitching staff wasn’t good enough to shoulder the load. Elias & Co. already decided to move on from former No. 1 pick Adley Rutschman, an All-Star catcher previously considered a foundational player, at the trade deadline. More significant moves could come this offseason. -- Castillo
19. St. Louis Cardinals
Record: 77-81
Previous ranking: 17
This rebuilding season has been an unqualified success for the Cardinals. If not for a leaky bullpen, their soft wild-card contention might have been a lot more solid. While bullpens are sometimes the final piece of the contention puzzle for a building team, that’s not always the case. Some clubs develop a bullpen-building process that takes effect even as the rest of the roster remains a work in progress. The Pirates of recent vintage are a good example.
Thus, the project of putting together a contention-worthy bullpen is a crucial one for the Chaim Bloom-led front office. Bloom was part of a Rays front office that annually churned out elite, no-name bullpens. However, during the four years that Bloom led the Red Sox front office, Boston ranked 24th in bullpen ERA (4.48) and middle-of-the-pack in save percentage. Good first year, but there is more to prove in St. Louis. -- Doolittle
20. Detroit Tigers
Record: 74-85
Previous ranking: 20
The Tigers will probably finish fourth in the AL in run differential, perhaps third if they pass the Red Sox, and will easily pace the Central by that measure. When you consider that, along with Detroit’s freakishly bad record in one- and two-run games (now 21-51) and the relatively short list of players on expiring deals (Jack Flaherty and Gleyber Torres, along with the retiring Justin Verlander), the Tigers are an obvious and very strong bounce-back candidate for the 2027 season. That doesn’t mean that president of baseball operations Scott Harris and his staff don’t have their work cut out for them when it comes to evaluating this lackluster season. Still, for the Tigers’ disappointed fans, it’s important to keep in mind that their team will be proceeding from a relative position of strength. -- Doolittle
21. Washington Nationals
Record: 75-84
Previous ranking: 23
In so many ways, the 2026 season was a success for the Nationals, who exceeded expectations this year, flirting with contention in the first half and seeing the development of players like CJ Abrams and James Wood into offensive stars. But the team’s pitching collapsed in the second half -- Washington’s second-half ERA of 4.49 ranks 25th. The Nationals locked down Cade Cavalli to a multiyear deal last week at the end of what has been a breakout season, but it’s clear that president of baseball operations Paul Toboni’s greatest challenge is to develop the sort of pipeline of pitching that will allow them to compete with the big-market teams in the division. -- Olney
22. Seattle Mariners
Record: 74-84
Previous ranking: 24
A year after falling one win short of the franchise’s first World Series appearance, the Mariners’ season will end Sunday with a whimper. The 2026 campaign will be remembered as the most disappointing one in franchise history.
Cal Raleigh’s drop-off from 60 home runs and an MVP runner-up finish was baffling. Julio Rodriguez regressed and still hasn’t made the superstar jump widely expected of him. Josh Naylor was a below-average hitter in the first year of his five-year contract. The starting rotation was not as good as advertised. Changes are inevitable, likely starting with manager Dan Wilson. But the Mariners can’t fire all of their players. They’ll need their core to bounce back from down seasons in order to rebound in 2027. -- Castillo
23. New York Mets
Record: 73-85
Previous ranking: 21
No one will go into the 2027 season under more pressure than David Stearns, the Mets’ head of baseball operations, following their collapse down the stretch in 2025 and the poor 2026 season. So it makes sense that he worked to keep someone he has a working relationship with in the managerial role, Andy Green, who had his interim tag removed and was hired to a three-year deal Tuesday. Steve Cohen’s comments on an SNY broadcast about needing new voices within the organization got the attention of a lot of rival executives, who wondered if the impact of Pete Alonso’s encore performance at Citi Field and the “Fire Stearns” chants last week made an impression on the owner. Under the circumstances, hiring Green seems like the right move for Stearns, the smart move. -- Olney
24. Minnesota Twins
Record: 75-84
Previous ranking: 22
The arrival of prospects Kaelen Culpepper, Walker Jenkins and Emmanuel Rodriguez has the Twins’ prospective 2027 position group in good shape even if veteran Josh Bell declines his mutual option and departs. The murkiest position is catcher, where Ryan Jeffers is likely headed for free agency, presumably after the Twins issue him a qualifying offer. The QO could limit Jeffers’ market, but probably not that much, as Jeffers looks like the best free agent catcher option out there. If he leaves, the Twins will need someone to pair with Caratini.
Long term, after drafting Vahn Lackey third in the most recent draft, the Twins seem in good shape with him, Eduardo Tait, Khadim Diaw and Carson Tinney all showing well in prospect rankings. Alas, none of that quartet is likely to be a 2027 solution. -- Doolittle
25. Cincinnati Reds
Record: 73-85
Previous ranking: 25
The ongoing maturation of Elly De La Cruz, as he edges toward his career prime, has provided ample reason to keep an eye on the Reds, even amid a last-place showing. Still, there have been enough trade rumors regarding the supremely talented shortstop to make you wonder just how long De La Cruz will be around.
Recent comments made by his agent, Scott Boras, don’t help. Boras suggested to reporters that a future foray into the open market made more sense for De La Cruz than a below-market extension. What does that mean for the Reds in the near term? For now, he has three more years of team control, so there’s no reason to be rash. Still, with this cloud starting to form over Great American Park, some sort of clarity about how the Reds plan to deal with their best player would be nice. -- Doolittle
26. Kansas City Royals
Record: 68-90
Previous ranking: 26
The Royals’ biggest offseason project will be to figure out their 2027 bullpen formula. That process begins with evaluating the relievers already on hand. Presumed closer Carlos Estevez had shoulder surgery -- bafflingly not until the second week of September -- and the Royals almost certainly won’t pick up their 2027 club option on him. Lucas Erceg looked lost before being shipped off to Omaha, but he performed well in Triple-A and his velocity upon his return to the majors has been at its highest level all year. Which Erceg is the real one? Is journeyman righty Nate Pearson a leverage option? Does Craig Kimbrel have anything left? The Royals will need relief help from outside the organization, but how much of it will depend on the outcome of these evaluations and others. -- Doolittle
27. San Francisco Giants
Record: 65-94
Previous ranking: 27
The general perception of San Francisco’s farm system is that it improved in 2026, and Bryce Eldridge established himself as a player the organization could build around. Beyond that, however, the Giants really haven’t progressed. They have a top-heavy payroll situation, with hundreds of millions owed to Rafael Devers, Willy Adames and Matt Chapman. The questions about manager Tony Vitello making the jump from college to professional baseball weren’t quelled by his first season with the Giants -- and neither were the questions about the man who hired him, Buster Posey, who is still relatively new to his front office role. -- Olney
28. Athletics
Record: 63-95
Previous ranking: 28
The A’s are stumbling to the finish line having lost 95 games. All-Star catcher Shea Langeliers recently returned from knee surgery, but several other prominent players remain on the IL, including Nick Kurtz, Tyler Soderstrom, Jacob Wilson, Brent Rooker, Luis Severino and Gage Jump. They’ll enter their season-ending series against the Astros with a negative-217 run differential -- the worst in the majors by 33 runs. With one season remaining before the A’s move to Las Vegas in 2028, they enter the winter in search of a general manager after David Forst’s departure in early August. Their offseason priorities are straightforward: Get healthy and improve a pitching staff that has a 5.43 ERA (29th) despite pitching half its games at the launchpad known as Sutter Health Park. -- Castillo
29. Los Angeles Angels
Record: 60-98
Previous ranking: 29
The Angels, despite 11 straight losing seasons, are the only franchise in the majors that has yet to post a 100-loss season. That could change this weekend in Seattle, where the Angels will need to win three of four games to avoid reaching the century mark. It’d be a fitting conclusion to Arte Moreno’s tenure as owner. Last month, Moreno agreed to sell controlling interest in the team to Stan Kroenke for a record valuation of $4 billion. Kroenke will take over a franchise that has not appeared in the postseason since 2014 and has not won a postseason game since 2009.
The first order of business this offseason will be hiring fired general manager Perry Minasian’s replacement. The team could also be in search of a manager to replace Kurt Suzuki, who is on a one-year contract. It is a transformative time in Anaheim. -- Castillo
30. Colorado Rockies
Record: 57-101
Previous ranking: 30
Colorado has compiled 100 losses for the fourth consecutive season; the last team to suffer 100-plus losses in five consecutive seasons were the Phillies, from 1938 to 1942. In Paul DePodesta’s first year of running Colorado’s baseball operations, there were some under-the-hood improvements: the biggest run differential improvement of all 30 teams in 2026, an improved farm system and some nice finds for the every-day lineup, like Jake McCarthy, TJ Rumfield and Connor Norby. There’s still a long way to go to competitive relevance for the Rockies, especially given the high bar required in the Dodgers’ NL West. -- Olney

item.content:encoded:
WEST SACRAMENTO — Mike Trout found a way to make history again on Wednesday night with a home run in the top of the fourth inning, but it wasn’t nearly enough as the Angels fell to the Athletics, 7-3, for their 98th loss of the season.
With his blast at Sutter Health Park, Trout has now hit a home run in 31 different MLB stadiums. With his 22nd homer of the season, he also has the most career home runs (44) against the A’s since the franchise moved to California in 1968, breaking his tie with Alex Rodríguez and Rafael Palmeiro.
Pittsburgh’s PNC Park, Chicago’s Wrigley Field, Atlanta’s Truist Park and Philadelphia’s Citizens Bank Park are the only active MLB ballparks where the three-time American League MVP has never homered.
Vaughn Grissom hit back-to-back homers with Trout, and the Angels threatened in the top of the fourth, but a potential game-tying home run off the bat of Christian Moore died on the warning track in center field. They added another run in the top of the fifth when Tyler Heineman scored on an RBI single by Grissom to get them within 5-3.
The last time Walbert Ureña pitched in Sacramento, he went five scoreless innings and didn’t walk a batter. Donovan Walton was also his teammate at the time. Ureña wasn’t nearly as sharp this time, giving up four runs in the first inning with the big blow being a three-run homer from Walton that snuck just inside the right field fair pole.
Ureña was pulled after four innings, giving up five runs (all earned) on seven hits with two strikeouts and one walk.
“Not the way that you want to finish, but that’s what happens when you give up 89 mph exit velo homers,” Ureña joked after the game.
His manager thought he could have been out of the game without allowing a single run, given the low exit velocity of the home run. Walton told Grissom that he broke his bat on the home run.
Heading into Wednesday’s slate of games, the Angels’ pitching staff had a 2.91 ERA since the beginning of August, the second-best mark in the majors. One of the reasons for that late-season surge has been Ureña, who finished his 2026 campaign with a 2.97 ERA.
The last major-league starter who was 22 or younger to record nine or more wins and have a sub-3.00 ERA was Pittsburgh Pirates ace Paul Skenes, who went 11-3 with a 1.96 ERA in 2024.
“To come back up and put that season together, I don’t know why they’re not talking more about [AL] Rookie of the Year,” Trout said after the game. “Everybody I talk to – opposing players – tell me that he’s got the nastiest stuff they’ve seen.”
Ureña also finished his season with 142 strikeouts, which ranks No. 2 in franchise history among players in their first major-league season behind Bo Belinsky’s 145 in 1962.
Even with the less-than-stellar end to his season, there has been plenty to build on heading into 2027.
“He’s got a lot of [José] Soriano in him,” A’s manager Mark Kotsay said Tuesday, comparing Ureña to a pitcher the Angels traded to the Toronto Blue Jays at the deadline in August. “A hard, heavy sinker that’s explosive. He attacks the zone, and I think that’s what stands out.”
At least one teammate pointed to Ureña’s slow heartbeat.
“The poise is there,” catcher Tyler Heineman said before Wednesday’s game. “He doesn’t really get rattled by anything. I think he’s made for the moment, even though he hasn’t had too many moments right now.”
Heineman also said the Ureña reminds him of Miami Marlins starter Sandy Alcantara, who is Ureña’s favorite pitcher. The key difference between the two is that Alcantara had a little more control coming up through the minor leagues, but the hard sinker and great secondary pitch are tough to ignore.
Ureña smiled after the game when he heard that comparison.
“He’s got one Cy Young [Award],” Ureña said. “He’s Dominican – Soriano too. He’s one of my brothers. He’s amazing. It feels good when they compare you with those guys.”
The young right-hander received plenty of praise from the clubhouse.
“Just fearlessness, man,” Angels relief pitcher Ryan Watson said. “He goes out there every five days and just pounds the strike zone.”
“Every time he takes the ball you feel really good,” Angels manager Kurt Suzuki said before the game. “He’s been really fun to watch.”
The next step for Ureña’s development will be learning how to harness his pitches on a consistent basis.
“His stuff moves so much,” Suzuki said. “Sometimes it’s hard to control. He’s learning how to harness it now, and when he gets a full understanding of how to harness [his pitches], the sky’s the limit.”
The A’s scored again in the second inning on a Henry Bolte double that scored Alika Williams from second base, but Ureña worked his way out of trouble in the third, stranding a runner at third base.
With the A’s leading 5-3 in the bottom of the sixth, Shea Langeliers roped a two-run double down the right field line to pad the margin.
Zach Neto was checked by the Angels’ training staff in the bottom of the first after a ground ball ricocheted off his glove and into left-center field, scoring the A’s first run of the game. Neto remained in the game. The play was scored a single and an RBI, with that decision leading to four runs being charged to Ureña in the first.
With four games left in a forgettable season, the Angels (60-98) need to win three games in Seattle this week to avoid the first 100-loss season in franchise history.

item.content:encoded:
Pittsburgh Pirates' starting pitcher Paul Skenes has come out and revealed that he believes his involvement in the World Baseball Classic is one reason to blame for his inconsistency and alarming drop in velocity in 2026.
Skenes spoke to the Pittsburgh Post Gazette on Monday and discussed his mechanics throughout the year, and the challenges that came with playing in the WBC before of the regular season.
"There are a lot of other factors, so I don't want to put everything on [the WBC]," Skenes said. "But I feel like that was kind of the root of it a little bit."
Of course the most glaring disparity in Skenes' game in 2026 was his drop in velocity. His fastball velocity averaged 96.8 mph in 2026, a big tick down from 98.1 mph in 2025 and 98.8 mph in 2024. As the season has gone on it has gotten worse as in his most recent start against the Kansas City Royals saw his fastball average 96.1 mph, and just 95.7 mph in his last start against Miami, which was the lowest in his career.
Although he does not regret his participation in the WBC for Team USA, Skenes did acknowledge that it did completely change his process in the offseason and how he did not have ample time to prepare his body for live innings so early in the year.
"Usually, that time of year, you're kind of ramping up and it's a little bit slow," Skenes said. "You can kind of get onto the slope and find your body. One live [batting practice], you're topping at 97, and then the next you're 98, 99. And that wasn't the case this year. … Looking back, I don't think that really helped."
Skenes went on to say that even in the early months of April and May where he looked like his usual dominant self, he wasn't satisfied with his mechanics and knew that something was off. The former National League Cy Young Award winner had a 1.09 ERA through eight starts in April and May.
"Even then, I didn't feel like I had my delivery," Skenes said. "It's just weird. It's easier to kind of put your finger on it after the fact than it is in the moment. It definitely affected the year. Unfortunately, I don't think I'm the only one. … Yeah, I don't know. [The WBC] definitely didn't make things easier."
Skenes has a 10-11 record this season with the Pirates and with a 3.91 ERA was often all over the place with pitch delivery, location, mechanics and the aforementioned velocity. He's hopeful to get back to his dominant self next season with a full and healthy offseason ahead of him, with regaining his mechanics being a top priority for the Pirates' ace.

The World Baseball Classic may have only been a couple of weeks long, but its impact was felt all season long.
Pittsburgh Pirates ace Paul Skenes has not been himself this year. His velocity has dipped, his command has been off, and after posting ERAs of 1.97 and 1.96, respectively, over the last two seasons, he has a 3.91 ERA this season. Why? Skenes said part of it was the World Baseball Classic.
"There are a lot of other factors, so I don’t want to put everything on that," Skenes told the Post-Gazette. "But I feel like that was kind of the root of it a little bit."

The World Baseball Classic ran from March 3 to March 17 this year, and Skenes said at that time of year, pitchers aren’t throwing at max effort.
"Usually, that time of year, you’re kind of ramping up and it’s a little bit slow. You can kind of get onto the slope and find your body," Skenes said. "One live (batting practice), you’re topping at 97 (mph), and then the next you’re 98, 99. And that wasn’t the case this year. ... Looking back, I don’t think that really helped."
Early in the season, Skenes pitched well despite not having his usual 98-mph fastball. In 2024, his rookie season, he averaged 98.8 mph, and last season he averaged 98.1 mph. This year, he is down to 96.8 mph.
Skenes didn’t have a set number for how hard he wanted to throw; he just wanted to throw harder. The 2025 NL Cy Young Award winner said he made mechanical adjustments to try to improve his velocity, but nothing came of them.
"Unfortunately, it’s probably going to take an offseason to get it back," Skenes said. "Yeah, it’s just tough."
Skenes didn’t blame all of his struggles on the World Baseball Classic, but he believed it had an impact. He also said he isn’t the only pitcher who was impacted.
"It definitely affected the year," Skenes said. "Unfortunately, I don’t think I’m the only one."
The Pirates hope their ace will have a strong offseason, return to form in 2027 and help the team make a postseason push, assuming there is a season amid the impending lockout.
